lesson.title: The Best-Case Number: Calculating Theoretical Yield
lesson.summary: Theoretical yield is the maximum possible mass of product a reaction could form, calculated entirely from the limiting reagent under the assumption that every bit of it converts perfectly into product.
lesson.body:
Once you know which reactant is limiting, you can ask a sharper question than just what runs out first: exactly how much product should this reaction produce, at best? That number is the theoretical yield, and it is a prediction, not a measurement. It assumes the reaction goes perfectly to completion, with no side reactions, no reversibility, and no product lost along the way. It is the ceiling that the real, messy laboratory result will be compared against.

The calculation is a direct extension of limiting reagent work. You take the moles of the limiting reagent, apply the mole ratio from the balanced equation to convert to moles of product, and then convert those moles of product into grams using the product's molar mass. It is the same mole ratio bridge you have used throughout stoichiometry, just aimed specifically at whichever reactant runs out first.

Here is a full worked example. Suppose 13.0 g of zinc metal reacts with an excess of hydrochloric acid according to Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2. Because HCl is explicitly in excess, zinc is the limiting reagent, and the entire calculation runs off the zinc. First convert mass to moles using zinc's molar mass of 65.38 g/mol: 13.0 g divided by 65.38 g/mol equals 0.1988 mol Zn. The balanced equation shows a 1 to 1 mole ratio between Zn and ZnCl2, so 0.1988 mol Zn produces 0.1988 mol ZnCl2. Finally, convert moles of product to grams using the molar mass of ZnCl2, which is 65.38 g/mol for zinc plus two times 35.45 g/mol for chlorine, or 136.28 g/mol. Multiplying, 0.1988 mol times 136.28 g/mol equals 27.1 g. The theoretical yield of ZnCl2 is 27.1 g.

Notice what this number does and does not claim. It does not say the reaction will produce 27.1 g. It says 27.1 g is the absolute maximum possible, the amount you would get if every single zinc atom found its way into a ZnCl2 molecule with nothing spilled, nothing left unreacted, and no competing reaction stealing atoms away. Real reactions almost never hit that ceiling. What actually comes out of the flask when you run this reaction on the bench is a different, separately measured quantity called the actual yield, which is the subject of the next chapter, and comparing the two is how chemists judge whether a reaction and a lab procedure performed well.
